High-velocity escapes like STF might constitute the 'inside-out' core collapse variant of the Carlson-Nummelova effect, resulting from the interaction between a protostar and surrounding envelope or perhaps resulting from the rapid spinning of a protostar influenced by a nearby disk or envelope. Further observations of similar high-velocity escapes from molecular clouds could follow up on this research, potentially leading to a deeper comprehension of this phenomenon.

We examine the underlying algorithmic model used in RAM with addition and establish a comprehensive time complexity classification for a broad class of typical mathematical functions. Our study reveals that many existing time complexity classifications for RAM are inconsistent and provides a unified framework for determining time complexities in this model.

To effectively match users with items in diverse real-world scenarios, various recommendation systems have been developed to take advantage of contextual information available in interaction data, like viewing histories, searching behaviors, and browsing paths. The contextual information can be harnessed using session-based recommendation models which learn to recommend items given user interaction data. The effectiveness of these methods significantly relies on how well they can identify users' and items' respective representations, and establish their mutual connections based on the available context. The emergence of graph neural networks (GNNs) offers promising prospects for improving the current session-based recommendation methods by capturing underlying graph patterns in the context. The key challenge with incorporating GNNs lies in choosing the input graph that best complements the given context for producing favorable outcomes. The graph choice also raises issues about potential biases, thereby necessitating methods that can neutralize any existing biases towards improving model performance. This research proposes a novel co-training framework called Self-Guided Graph Co-Training (SGGT) which addresses these challenges by simultaneously training two GNN models on node and graph representations alongside each other. The key components of the SGGT framework is a novel node representation learning model that combines mutual learning with graph information, and a corresponding graph representation learning model that adapts the input graph based on node representations. The capacity of the proposed model to improve session-based recommendation was demonstrated through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, and the results show that SGGT surpasses state-of-the-art baselines by a

The concept of reversible source encoding has been introduced as a dual to variable-length source encoding, with binary reversible arithmetic coding serving as a primary example. Our research expands on this idea by developing the first practical, asymmetric reversible codes utilizing non-binary alphabets. Specifically, we present the reversible least common multiple (RLCM) code, which can also be applied in irreversible form (LCM code) with superior performance compared to existing approaches like arithmetic and gamma codes. When considering the irreversible LCM code, our findings reveal that it achieves the best known rate-distortion performance among all fixed and variable-rate codes with a specific memory trade-off. Furthermore, the reversible LCM code offers an alternative with lower storage requirements, which performs comparably to binary reversible arithmetic coding in terms of distortion and storage. Additionally, the reversible LCM code exhibits superior performance in both irreversible and reversible forms compared to existing codes like arithmetic and gamma codes.

Recent research in topological graph theory has led to significant breakthroughs by linking subcomplexes of network shapes to distinct topological invariants. Building upon this work, we identify and characterize unique differential forms associated with each subcomplex of network shapes, establishing a geometric framework for understanding Feynman integrals through the perspective of differential forms on complex shapes. This is further demonstrated by introducing a novel differential equation that generalizes previous findings on specific graph types, revealing its connection to the homology classes of graph-related complexes known as good swamps.

In various cognitive and computational systems, objects are processed using sequential or simultaneous presentations. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) mimic the temporal processing of cognitive systems, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Our study aligned objects with random textures and assessed how different visual cues (lines, colors, shapes) interact through interaction effects. The interaction between lines and colors, but not shapes, influenced learning in RNNs. These findings suggest that recurrent neural networks like the Simple RNN, LSTM, and GRU learn to process objects by combining lines and colors, as evidenced by model interpretations.

In one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems with discrete point-gap topology, the topological characteristics associated with localized modes at individual points exhibit an exceptionally robust trend. We have performed an in-depth analysis of how these topological properties might change when such systems undergo point-interaction fusion, resulting in the emergence of a more comprehensive topological structure. Notably, our findings indicate that the stability of exceptional points, where two localized modes converge, is linked to an intricate balance of system parameters and interaction strength. Consequently, even minimal deviations can trigger exceptional point crossing and collapse, along with the associated mode fusion. In an attempt to mitigate this vulnerability, we have developed a method for transferring the topological structure from one-dimensional systems to extended multi-dimensional systems, effectively diminishing the risk of point-gap topology diminution in the process.

This work presents novel designs for Golay complementary structures through the use of polyphase sequences, thereby expanding the applicability of Golay complementary matrices. A generalized framework for the Golay complementary matrix is established, allowing for the generation of distinct complementary matrices. Notably, the proposed designs yield sequences with multiple phase codes, offering advantages in areas such as spread spectrum communications and test pattern generation. The paper also examines the possible phase codes that can be incorporated into the proposed Golay complementary structures, including those based on Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, phasors, and pseudorandom number generators. The maximum number of phase codes that can be employed in a single sequence is determined to be three.

This study explores the hypothetical broad Higgs boson scenario, examining its implications of a non-zero width on the $H \rightarrow WW^{\ast}$ process. To to this end, the theoretical team, particularly focused on the $pp \to IVV^{\ast} \to LLVV^{\ast}$ signal, linked with the $pp \to WW^{\ast}$ reference process, aimed to quantify the relative impact of a broad Higgs boson on the $H \rightarrow WW^{\ast}$ signal. To accomplish this, the team evaluated the ratio of the $H \rightarrow WW^{\ast}$ signal to the $WW^{\ast}$ reference process, both of which were produced and analyzed using the ATLAS and CMS experiment's latest, most sophisticated methods. To determine the relative impact of a broad Higgs boson, the team resorted to the comparison of the $H \rightarrow LLVV^{\ast}$ and $WW^{\ast}$ reference signals, both of which were computed with the latest, most advanced parton distribution functions. To validate the effectiveness of their approach, the team engaged in a comprehensive study, accompanied by a comprehensive presentation, in which they presented their findings, as well as the results of their studies on the determinability of unusual $H \rightarrow VV$ connections.

Hyperspectral imaging technology, which exceeds human vision, has garnered attention from researchers and practitioners alike. Despite its benefits, hyperspectral data analysis remains a difficult task due to the high dimensionality of the data. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel approach that utilizes a deep convolutional autoencoder to recognize alterations in hyperspectral images without manual annotation. By fusing spatial and spectral features through a fully connected layer, our model effectively integrates various feature extractors and encoders, ultimately leading to improved alteration detection performance. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, confirming its efficacy in unsupervised hyperspectral alteration detection.

We begin by establishing an explicit formula for the sum of all square numbers $m^2$ that are less than or equal to a given positive integer $n$, where $m$ ranges from $1$ to $n-1$. We then derive a similar formula for the sum of all triangular numbers $m(m+1)/2$ that are less than or equal to $n$, which is followed by a formula for the sum of all fifth powers $\boxed{m}^5$ that are less than or equal to $n$, where $m$ ranges from $1$ to $n-4$. These formulas have been consistently provided in the form of differences of powers, which is in line with the findings of the 18th Catalan's Number having a representation as the sum of all fifth powers that are less than or equal to 41. We also provide an explicit representation for the sum of all seventh powers $\boxed{m}^7$ that are less than or equal to 189. We believe that with further research, we can generalise these results to higher dimensional cases as well.

Quantum bits stored in the valley states of excitons exhibit great potential for robust and persistent data storage, yet efficient and controlled interaction with these valley states remains a significant challenge in practical quantum computing implementations. Researchers have now successfully transferred spin from a silicon donor to a silicon vacancy in a silicon substrate using optically detected magnetic resonance. This breakthrough, facilitated by a silicon nanowire, enabled the transfer of spin from a silicon vacancy to a silicon donor, and subsequently, the emission of this transferred spin into a silicon exciton valley state. This novel approach may enable the development of compact and stable quantum memory based on silicon for future quantum computing applications.

Many optimization problems naturally lend themselves to more efficient solution strategies that take into account uncertainty and limited computational resources, making classic model-based methods less suitable and potentially costly. Recent years have seen the emergence of novel solution methods, such as optimization with quantization or compression, but these techniques have largely been confined to fixed-point signal processing contexts. Our proposal LibOPT addresses this gap by providing a flexible framework supporting three distinct open-source implementation approaches for developing new methodological contributions. Building on the strengths of existing approaches - Zinpro and OptPro, - we introduce a pioneering work on three novel methods: K-Means with Ambiguity Removal, Hyperbolic Optimization with Compression, and Vector Quantization-based Optimization. Our framework's comprehensive toolset includes an advanced solver written in C based on Knuth's algorithm, symbolic mathematical computing via SymPy, and a Python-based interactive shell with integrated debugging facilities.

Given a subvariety V that is uniformly closed under finite morphisms within a fixed dimension, we define the transferability degree of V as the largest possible integer value t, such that V can incorporate any algebraic subset of that dimension with a morphism that has a specific invariant property. We establish that for a wide range of specific algebraic varieties, such as toric varieties and orbifolds with compactification, the transferability degree is infinite. Additionally, we demonstrate that varieties with infinite transferability degree possess certain equivalent characteristics, including the ability for finite morphisms to be expressed algebraically and the capacity for algebraic reworking in any dimension. This discovery specifically confirms that toric varieties and orbifolds with compactification have their finite morphisms expressed algebraically.

In this paper, we explore the nature of quantum entities in the context of a non-commutative spacetime characterized by a non-zero minimum measurement uncertainty for adjacent spatial measurements. Utilizing the functional Schrödinger equation, we demonstrate that there exists a vast range of possible particle states that adhere to the principles of quantum mechanics, particularly regarding the relationship between position and momentum operators. However, the multitude of identically structured quantum states raises an ontological dilemma: can we consider all quantum entities as identical objects? To address this concern, we suggest a dual approach, combining both the understanding of particle trajectories within a non-commutative spacetime and the replication of quantum states through position-momentum transformations. These theories prompt a broader inquiry: are quantum entities truly distinct from their counterparts in a commutative spacetime? To resolve this enigma, we examine the diversity of quantum states in relation to position-momentum transformations and the reproduction of quantum particles via spacetime non-commutativity. Ultimately, the uncertainty principle's influence on quantum entities complicates our understanding of their individuality, raising fundamental questions about their distinctiveness and the nature of their existence.

We have developed a novel technique for 3D spatial mapping of electrical charge conduction in single-crystalline materials. This involves coating the material with a thin, semi-transparent photoconductive layer, after which we apply a small amount of laser light to one side. As charge becomes trapped and releases near the illumination site, the resulting transient current signal is measured and analyzed to reconstruct the 3D charge distribution. This approach enables us to map charges on the nanoscale by utilizing the unique properties of photoconductive materials to detect charge injection or mobile charge generation under controlled conditions. As a test of this method's effectiveness, we successfully created three-dimensional images of oxygen-related defect formation in synthetic single-crystalline diamond by combining the proposed technique with focused ultraviolet light illumination.

Social media platforms are facing significant issues due to the presence of toxic content like harassment, bullying, and misogyny. These problems not only create a toxic online environment for users but also have real-world consequences, potentially leading to increased mental health problems for those exposed. Detecting and classifying toxic content, particularly misogyny, on social media has become a pressing concern for researchers, as identifying it manually is nearly impossible due to its vast scale. Existing studies have primarily focused on English-based systems, leaving systems for detecting misogyny in other languages underrepresented. In an effort to fill this gap, we introduce a pioneering work for detecting and classifying misogynistic content in the Arabic language. Our proposed system is a deep multi-task network that simultaneously tackles three key tasks: detecting toxic content, detecting misogynistic content, and categorizing the severity of that content. To ensure accuracy, we fine-tune BERT, a popular language model, by incorporating it into a transformer-based multi-task framework. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this system, with a high F1 score of 71.67% for misogynicity detection and a macro F1 score of 70.78% for severity classification. These scores significantly outperform existing models, with a comparative study showing that our results surpass the performance of other state-of-the-art models.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations, referred to as the BSDEs, which are based on an advanced generator compared to standard stochastic differential equations. Key aspects of our research involve verifying the existence and uniqueness of the solution, establishing different types of continuity for the generator, and exploring the relationship between the solution and its corresponding auxiliary equation. Additionally, we introduce a delayed generator class and prove similar results for this variant, before providing a key application that links it to a related fractional Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation.

Despite the rapid growth in safety controllers for autonomous systems, implementing them in complex real-world setups remains a significant challenge due to the diversity of possible environments and limitations in modeling accuracy. This research introduces a novel approach that combines both offline planning and online adaptation to acquire resilient controllers capable of withstanding unexpected conditions and system component failures. By utilizing a simplified model of the system, an optimal control strategy is calculated, and the controller is adjusted in real-time based on the actual system performance and environmental variations encountered during operation. This approach is exemplified in a case study involving an autonomous driving system within a dynamically changing road network.

A newly developed framework, known as UfOC, aims to provide a comprehensive model for encoded caching schemes and decentralized computation schemes. The framework, UfOC, consists of three key components: a source that distributes information, a decoder with limited capacity, and a encoder with limited capacity. By doing so, the framework, UfOC, seeks to optimize trade-off between information loss and encoding efficiency. The effectiveness of the framework, UfOC, is demonstrated through its application to a range of established schemes as well as its potential to yield novel schemes. The framework, UfOC, also facilitates an intrinsic connection between encoded caching schemes and decentralized computation schemes. The framework, UfOC, also establishes a critical relationship between the two schemes, thereby providing a universal model for their interaction. The results of the application of the framework, UfOC, to a range of existing schemes, suggest that these schemes can be optimized to yield improved performance. The framework, UfOC, thus holds the potential to yield novel schemes and improve the performance of existing ones.

We develop a framework for formalizing the Scott model of PCF within a dependent type theory, assuming univalence as a hypothesis. Our formalization closely mirrors Scott's original construction but adapts it to incorporate the principles of univalent dependent types. By doing so, we demonstrate that the Scott model can be grounded in a rigorous theoretical framework. Additionally, as a practical outcome of this study, we implement the formalization in the Coq proof assistant, utilizing univalent-dependent types to define the PCF model.

This study employs the concept of "Bianchi type" introduced in Deligne's work, combined with the specific properties of unramified Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ to the $2k$-dimensional space of cusp forms. It demonstrates the existence of a type 'B' representation that is irreducible when 'k' is greater than 1.

This research presents a novel secure control approach for mobile robotic arms, prioritizing flexibility and efficiency. Unlike existing methods, which frequently rely on conservative assumptions and neglect key factors, our proposed control strategy considers and addresses the interactions between robotic movement, electric security, and environmental constraints. By developing a secure control framework that includes a security monitor and a predictive policy, we have created an innovative solution that seamlessly integrates robotic movement optimization while guaranteeing electric security. Real-world validation on a Zebrobotic limb showcases the efficacy and efficiency of our secure control approach.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based techniques for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction method.

Researchers have successfully adapted the discrete time Schrödinger equation, originally designed for quantum systems, to the context of Bose-Einstein condensates. This involves transforming key operators from their standard form to a discrete representation. The resulting study examines how these new operators mimic the original ones in the limit of very small grid spacing. Furthermore, evidence supports the validity of the discrete representation by comparing numerically derived values with their analytical counterparts for specific BEC configurations.

This study examines the distinctness of meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold into a complex projective space, particularly in cases where the mappings are non-dominant. Our research builds upon previous work discussed at the conference "Complex Analysis in several complex variables: Proceedings of the international conference at 100 years of Kungliga Svenska Vetenskapssocieteten" held in Stockholm, August 26-29, 2014.

In the context of practical applications related to algebraic geometry, ideal membership, dimension, and singularities of a projective polynomial system depend on identifying nondegenerate components of the system's zeros. We have developed a new signature-based method to determine nondegenerate regions of a projective polynomial system, along with corresponding dimension estimates. This method leverages a signature analysis algorithm previously established. The proposed approach is demonstrated through a relevant example.

This presentation outlines the current method for identifying direct photons in heavy-ion collisions, specifically focusing on low-momentum direct photons. The analysis utilizes data from the PHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and accounts for the material present in the beam pipe.

A significant problem known as Turan's Tetrahedron Challenge has garnered considerable interest over the centuries. The problem, proposed by Turan in 1967, asked for the minimum number of incident edge triples in a graph that contain at least one clique of size three, and this number has been steadily increased by prominent mathematicians throughout the years. The problem, although solved for certain graph properties in the past, has resisted solution for its general form until now. The authors, inspired by earlier work in entropy and hypergraph removal lemmas, employ these concepts to demonstrate that the current record set by Gyarfas, and verified to hold for graphs with every pair of adjacent vertices connected to at least one common vertex, is in fact true for all graphs. Additionally, the authors utilize this result to solve another long-standing problem, and further extend their application to quantify the minimum number of edge triples in graphs that contain at least one general hyperedge of a specific size.

When displaying vector maps on devices with limited rendering capabilities, aliasing often occurs, causing poor visual experience. Typical solutions involve removing or simplifying line segments, but these methods impair the clarity of map features. To address this issue, we've developed an anti-aliasing technique specifically designed for line connections, allowing for seamless rendering on devices with limited resources. Our approach leverages the map's hierarchical structure, incorporating color information from neighboring elements to eliminate aliasing. To achieve this, we employed two effective methods: pixel splitting and shader-based anti-aliasing. Through testing, we've shown that our technique can enhance visual quality, and we've also optimized it for optimal performance. Additionally, we've addressed potential issues related to color and implemented a feature that automatically detects and adjusts rendering settings for complex patterns. As a result, our anti-aliasing technique can be used in a wide range of real-world mapping applications without compromising performance.

A recently introduced transcendental RBF for multivariate functions has proven to be an attractive option due to its superior convergence properties and robustness in dealing with noisy data. However, the operator derived from this choice exhibits unbounded values, which poses a problem for use in finite element methods that demand variational formulations. To address this issue, a modified quasi-interpolation operator is presented, which maintains a stable form and is supported by a comprehensive theoretical framework. The proof that this operator satisfies the U-form condition, a crucial requirement for variational interpolation operators, involves a novel approach that differs from standard Radon-Berens techniques. The findings demonstrate that the operator possesses a continuous version in $C^0(\Omega)$ and an $L_p^p$ norm, and ensures that data is preserved with an $L_p$ error, with a corresponding error estimate also provided. The results validate the suitability of the transcendental RBF for variational methods, opening up a range of potential applications.

Pulsar wind bubbles are formed when expanding plasmoids interact with interstellar gas, creating distinct X-ray and gamma-ray emission patterns. Pulsar A, a bright gamma-ray source, is associated with the pulsar wind bubble G116.1+1.0, shared by the nearby young pulsar PSR J1953+49.1. As the pulsar ages, its wind bubble likely merges with surrounding supernova remnant fragments, evident in the large, composite structure visible in X-ray images. This association is confirmed by gamma-ray emission originating from the wind bubble's edges and incorporating the pulsar's gamma-ray emission. This merged wind bubble shares characteristics with those of the Crab Nebula, resulting from the interaction of a pulsar wind on an expanding supernova remnant. Systems like this, composed of wind bubbles and pulsar pairs, are potential gamma-ray sources.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have excelled in weather picture classification, but they have yet to be thoroughly evaluated against other machine learning techniques in this domain. A systematic assessment of CNNs has been hampered by a lack of standard, widely available climate image datasets. To address this issue, we introduce the ClimateCats dataset, which consists of 38,000 high-quality images representing 10 distinct climate types, along with related metadata. This dataset enables climate classification to be performed through image recognition. Due to the variability and subjectiveness of weather data, we employ multi-instance learning and human annotation to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the dataset. Additionally, we develop a novel data augmentation strategy, combining global and local operations, to effectively increase the dataset size and combat overfitting. To our knowledge, the ClimateCats dataset constitutes one of the largest collections of labeled climate images, and it surpasses the performance of leading CNN models, including the MobileNetV2, ResNet, and SeNet networks, as well as a newly proposed Dilated Convolutional Network (DCN).

The world is experiencing an unprecedented shift towards adopting sustainable practices due to climate change. Countries are working to reduce carbon emissions, yet the pace of progress is hindered by a lack of understanding climate science, misinformation, and conflicting political priorities. The climate crisis is complicated by the fragmentation of its various components, which are influenced by distinct social norms. Research, for instance, upholds high standards of evidence and rigor, whereas economic decisions prioritize immediate financial gains over long-term environmental benefits. The public's climate perceptions are shaped by personal experiences and media coverage, which can be manipulated by politicians for political gain. The consequences of climate change, including severe weather events and biodiversity loss, have a disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations. This research highlights the distinct social norms of its different aspects, discusses the influence of external factors like political affiliations and economic interests, and explores the interactions between these elements. By recognizing and clarifying these interactions, we aim to uncover the underlying dynamics of the climate crisis and identify potential entry points for transformation.

Soft grippers excel at handling delicate objects, but their flexible structure makes it difficult to predict their behavior and plan movements. To address this issue, researchers developed a virtual model of a multi-fingered gripper consisting of elastic fingers and a moving base. They integrated a novel control system using the Koopman operator method to optimize movement planning and regulation of the gripper's fingers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in capturing finger dynamics and achieving desired finger positions. Additionally, researchers applied their model to a real-world application, successfully guiding a gripper to grasp small tools in a robotic hand.

Inspired by the organic growth in natural evolution, we introduce a generalized gradient descent framework, adaptable to various underlying systems and their corresponding dynamics. This approach is based on the geometric relationships between the gradient flow and a downward-pointing vector field, defined on the target function's domain. We demonstrate that existing gradient-based optimization methods can be reinterpreted through this framework, encompassing geometric statistics, mean field game theory, and beyond. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which our framework generates well-known optimization algorithms, including stochastic gradient descent, Newton's method, and their respective variants.

Initially believed to be an unusual quasar based on its bright radio emission, more in-depth analysis has now revealed that the source's intense radiation has a dual origin. In addition to the expected activity from an supermassive black hole, the data also suggest the presence of another component, likely a compact radio object. This new object's properties resemble those of megahertz peaked spectrum sources. Research indicates that these sources are predominantly young and rapidly evolving. Therefore, it is thought that the intense activity in these sources declines at an exponential rate and their number density decreases with age. Based on this information, it is estimated that the likelihood of a particular source being an SMBBH or radio object is around 3 in 1000. The data suggests that the majority of powerful quasars at z > 4.5 are actually dominated by radio objects rather than BBH activity. Further study is needed to confirm these findings.

Lung cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally, can be effectively combated through early detection. The advancement of CT technology has significantly improved the accuracy of lesion classification, yet challenges persist due to image quality issues, diverse tumor types, and limited data availability. To address these problems, this research develops a SEU (Squeeze and Expand Unit)-based education framework that integrates information from multiple modalities, enhancing the capability of classifiers to accurately locate, categorize, and count lung carcinomas. The proposed framework consists of three key components: a feature extractor, a data augmentation module, and an education process, all working in harmony to optimize performance. The efficacy of this method is validated against the Lung Cancer dataset of the Medical Image Classification challenge on CodeHub, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches by a substantial margin of 8.07% and achieving state-of-the-art AUC of 93.70%.

In tasks that require extensive knowledge, prior experience is necessary to make informed decisions. Reinforcement Learning (RL) integrates learning from past experiences to shape future actions. For RL to be effective, a comprehensive update of the agent's understanding of the world is required after each experience. Natural Language State Description (NLSD) plays a vital role in this process, enabling the agent to learn from the context and make informed decisions. This paper discusses NLSD, highlighting its key aspects and the various methods employed to implement it in RL systems.

A breakthrough in understanding the universe's long-term growth lies in analyzing the temperature of intergalactic gas, which can be obtained by analyzing the absorption spectra of high-redshift quasars. Despite previous methods' limitations and high requirements due to the need for manual data processing, a new artificial intelligence (AI) powered approach enables the analysis of large quasar datasets without human intervention. The AI model, comprised of two neural networks, accurately predicts the absorption line parameters and thermodynamic properties of the intergalactic gas, thereby facilitating the comparison of datasets obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope and XMM-Newton Space Telescope. Moreover, the AI model enables the comparison of different quasar datasets, thereby allowing researchers to obtain precise estimates of the universe's temperature and other critical cosmological parameters.

Consider a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ and its tensor algebra $T(V)$. The derivation algebra of $T(V)$ is given by $\text{Der}(T(V))$, consisting of linear operators that satisfy specific properties with respect to the algebra's operations. By exploring the properties of these operators, one can establish a homomorphism $\Phi$ from the Lie algebra of $\text{End}(V)$ to $\text{Der}(T(V))$. The paper examines the basis of $\frak h$ generated by $\Phi(\frak h)$ and seeks to identify simple modules over $\frak h$ that are excluded from the Lie algebra. The investigation reveals a complete classification of simple $U(\frak h)$-excluded modules and establishes relationships between these modules and the Julia sets associated with rational maps. Additionally, the analysis provides insights into the complexities of the Lie algebra's properties by linking them to problems in complex analysis and fractal geometry.

Social media monitoring, specifically through Twitter, has become an essential tool for businesses and organizations to gain a deeper understanding of public opinion. The constantly updating flow of data on Twitter necessitates the use of sentiment analysis to translate opinions into actionable insights. The diverse character limitations of Twitter present unique analysis challenges, and the noise often found in tweets further complicates the process. To effectively analyze sentiment from the platform, we undertook a study and developed an LSTM-based framework, taking into account the inherent characteristics of Twitter data and incorporating noise handling to enhance accuracy. The framework's performance was validated through cross-validation, and comparisons were made with popular off-the-shelf sentiment analysis tools.

Recently, open-domain conversation models have gained significant attention due to their versatility in creating natural language interactions. To achieve expertise in these conversations, it is necessary for the conversational agents to adapt to various roles, allowing them to effectively engage in relevant discussions. In this research, we introduce a framework called RODCF, which enables role-defined open-domain conversations by utilizing samples to define conversation topics and assigning roles through topic matching. Additionally, we conducted comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, and the results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms compared to baseline models and is capable of sustaining conversations with impressive coherence and relevance. Furthermore, an in-depth case study reveals that RODCF is highly effective in building conversations around given topic roles, and further analysis indicates that the model's performance can be enhanced through data augmentation and the optimization of model parameters for specific roles.

The concept of gravitational waves memorization proposes that there could be residual gravitational waves from the early universe that have not been dissipated yet, given that inflationary cosmological models often involve an anisotropic graviational field. This persistent gravitational memory might be observable in the form of low-frequency gravitational waves with a broad frequency range spanning from $10^{-16}$ Hz to $10^{-14}$ Hz. The likelihood of these low-frequency gravitational waves exists across various inflationary models, and their power spectrum displays a characteristic scale-invariant property, and their production likelihood exists across various inflationary models, and their power spectrum displays a characteristic scale-invariant property, and their presence could be detected using instruments such as LISA, and their presence could be detected using instruments such as LISA.

Introducing an almost parallel lattice of extra dimensions at a PeV-scale, we propose a theoretical framework where the supersymmetry breaking occurs due to a phase shift between the compactified dimensions. This model also predicts the existence of extra gauge bosons within the extra dimensions, heavy gauge bosons born from gravity waves, and pairs of neutralinos comprised of $SU(2)_L, U(1)_Y, U(1)_{B-L}$ components, all of which are accessible via direct detection experiments. Additionally, the scenario is corroborated by an observation matching the Carrollian cosmology within the gravity wave spectrum by CMB-scale physics, as well as a black hole creation possibility through a four-dimensional brane, where the dark matter in question might also be produced.

A fundamental inquiry in artificial intelligence, encompassing both symbolic and subsymbolic approaches, seeks to decipher causal relationships in complex systems. This study integrates disparate lines of research by combining the capacity for causal inference with the ability to model signaling interactions through game theory. We demonstrate that symbolic causal graphs can be translated into equilibrium mechanisms, which facilitate transparent communication among agents working towards mutually beneficial outcomes. Conversely, we show that observable payoff streams can be interpreted as symbolic causal influences, effectively bridging subsymbolic and symbolic representations. Experimental evaluations, conducted using simplified signaling scenarios, reveal that symbolic representations gain precision when integrated with subsymbolic mechanisms. Specifically, the gain in symbolic expression accuracy comes from the mechanism's equilibria, which are calculated using techniques from convex geometry and combinatoric optimization. These findings offer a novel framework for artificial intelligence, merging the strengths of symbolic and subsymbolic AI to tackle complex problems.

Information retrieval technology has expanded rapidly into diverse industries such as e-commerce, advertising, and communications, all of which involve predicting user behavior to optimize interactions and achieve better results. The demand for accurate term forecasting has increased significantly, which is essential for managing user expectations and preventing over-promising and under-delivering. Existing research on term forecasting focuses on modeling user behavior based on historical data but overlooks the need to consider and forecast varying levels of document engagement. This paper proposes a new approach to term forecasting by incorporating the Naive Bayes classifier and Latent Information Retrieval models to enhance forecasting precision and adaptability. Furthermore, it introduces a hybrid framework that combines the strengths of both models, leveraging their distinct capabilities to achieve improved accuracy and forecasting ranges.

Recent research has focused on creating interactive systems that generate refined suggestions based on users' prior choices. Existing models, however, typically represent user preferences using a single score and generate suggestions in two discrete phases, which can result in suboptimal suggestions. For instance, if a user's initial preference is high but later becomes lower, existing models may initially prioritize similar items but eventually dislike them. To address this issue, we propose a new system that employs a dynamic representation of suggestion rank and separates suggestion generation into two phases based on the strength of prior preferences. By doing so, we ensure that the system initially prefers similar items and subsequently disfavors them when the user's preferences weaken. When compared to the top-performing system, our model demonstrates improved performance across a range of testing conditions and outperforms it by at least 10% in scenarios where the user's preferences weaken.

Observing active particles, such as swimming bacteria or moving colloids, in a diverse range of environments has generated both curiosity and practical concerns regarding their behavior. In response to their surrounding environment's energy variations, these particles may experience a force known as the activity gradient force, significantly influencing their movement. In this study, we employ theoretical and experimental methods to investigate this force's effect on active particles demonstrating Brownian motion. By integrating activity measurements into a dynamic model, we analyzed the particle dynamics, which were later confirmed through experiments involving active bacteria and active colloids in a dynamic setting.

This research introduces a novel approach to simulating single-phase flow through three-dimensional fracturing networks by adopting a discrete fracture model. To achieve this, the proposed method extends the finite element method in three dimensions to include mapping from a non-conforming grid of volumes to a conforming network of pipes. To validate the technique, precise flow and conveyance calculations are performed in simple scenarios, including cases with singular fractures, multiple fractures, individual fracture branching models, and complex networks of fractures. Results from these tests are compared against existing literature and the extended method's efficiency is demonstrated through its application in a complex example involving over a million elements.

This research paper proposes an innovative approach to maintain cellular structure integrity and prevent drone collisions by leveraging point set alignment, drawing from similarities between drone trajectories and shifting cell patterns. To achieve precise alignment, the algorithm minimizes drone flight paths, treating them as a geometric optimization problem, and tests various methods to estimate cell centroid positions from aerial drone images. The study demonstrates that using the centroid of a drone's capture radius (the "bubble" around its camera) as the cell feature yields the best results in aligning cellular structures and preventing collisions. The research showcases that this approach can effectively replicate shifting cell patterns observed on the ground from the perspective of flying drones.

A graph sequence consists of a collection of graphs connected by edge insertions or deletions, corresponding to a specific mutation scheme. The Seidel energy of a graph measures the variance of its Seidel matrix eigenvalues, which can be employed to quantify the differences between adjacent graphs in a sequence. In this study, the range of the Seidel energy is determined for a particular type of graph sequence known as Krasnyporov sequences, which are characterized by the emergence of new perfect matchings through edge deletions. Additionally, the paper specifies the Seidel energy values for linear trees and provides hypotheses regarding the Seidel energy for certain star trees.

The paper addresses the optimal control issue for linear stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion, with a unique optimal sink solution characterized by a mean-field interaction through its trajectory. By applying the variational approach and Lagrange multiplier method, we establish the FBSDEs that define the optimal control's first-order conditions, before ultimately deriving a stochastic differential equation that represents the optimal trajectory. Notably, our approach differs from standard stochastic maximum principle applications by prioritizing the initial equation's optimality conditions over its dual counterparts.

We're investigating the unique finite-band elliptic operators of the Dirac type within the context of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$. These operators can be represented as a sum of a self-adjoint part and a non-self-adjoint part. Given that the non-self-adjoint component is relatively compact, we develop a method to compute the $m$-th eigenvalue of the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator for any positive or negative value of $m$. These eigenvalues are expressed as a function of two variables, $t$ and $s$, where $t$ represents the magnitude of the off-diagonal matrix and $s$ represents the trace of the off-diagonal matrix. The structure of these variables allows us to apply techniques from elliptic theory and singular Sturm-Liouville problems to study the operator's spectrum. Specifically, we create a transform that maps the original operator to one with band-like structure, thereby simplifying our analysis and enabling detailed calculations of eigenvalues. Additionally, we investigate the operator's boundary quotient and the behavior of Dirac eigenvalues as they approach the boundary of the essential spectrum.

The integration of vehicles into ad-hoc networks is gaining traction as a means to enhance network connectivity and capacity in urban settings. A two-tier approach to vehicular networks is being explored, which incorporates vehicles serving as relays for both mobile devices and other vehicles. Focusing on the intersections of these vehicle networks, this study examines the performance of these diverse networks under different scenarios, incorporating vehicle density, vehicle speed, and the availability of roadside access points. Modeling, simulations, and analytical methods are utilized to evaluate and compare the performance of these diverse networks, with results indicating that vehicle density has a significant impact on network performance, while changes in speed have varying effects depending on whether there are available roadside access points or not.

Wikipedia's potential for spreading misinformation and absorbing false information has prompted a need for identifying and categorizing low-quality articles. Research on Wikipedia's editing behavior has been shown to hold valuable insights in achieving this goal, and our study aims to contribute to the advancement of this field by developing a method for pinpointing low-quality articles through analysis of editing patterns. We have derived a set of distinguishing features from editing behavior and employed these characteristics to design and train a machine learning model for automatically classifying articles. The proposed method has demonstrated success in different machine learning frameworks and has surpassed the performance of leading manual assessment methods, indicating its potential utility in augmenting existing quality assessment processes on Wikipedia.

Achieving accurate bug detection in commercial software through decision-based black-box testing is challenging, especially when there's a limited number of available bug examples to train models. The scarcity of data and unreliable annotations in real-world bug data make it difficult to obtain high-quality labeled samples for model improvement. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel approach, Decision-Based Black-Box Knowledge Distillation, which enables the effective transfer of knowledge from experienced models to inexperienced models in a black-box test framework. The approach has been validated through experiments on real-world bug data from Open Source, and the results show that it outperforms baseline models by a significant margin, with an average improvement of 8.5% in accuracy.

The initial observation of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays is made utilizing 358 pb$^{-1}$ of data collected with the LHCb detector at 7 and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions. Branching fractions for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays are calculated to be (3.7$^{+1.1+0.1}$$_{-0.9-0.1}$) $\times 10^{-4}$ and (3.4$^{+1.3+0.2}$$_{-1.2-0.2}$) $\times 10^{-4}$, respectively, with corresponding upper limits set at 4.5 $\times 10^{-4}$ and 4.3 $\times 10^{-4}$ in addition to previously published results. The observed anomalies in $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decays previously reported are not confirmed.

We've extended geometric T-duality to generalized tori with singularities by adapting the Poisson-Lie deformation of T-duality, incorporating twisted harmonic forms and Chern-Simons connections. Our work generalizes T-duality to geometries with singularities and addresses the issue of the de Rham cohomology dimension discrepancy to achieve this. Furthermore, we've applied the procedure to examples of singularized tori, including the twisted torus with Abel-Jacobi map and the torus with weighted punctures.

A key aspect of large-scale astronomical data analysis lies in effectively training models to capture complex, highly detailed astronomical data. Since astronomical observations are often made by multiple instruments, we've developed a novel method that leverages the strengths of collaborative learning without relying on expert input, thereby fully utilizing the available data. Our approach employs a novel co-training strategy based on deep convolutional neural networks, where two models are simultaneously trained on two datasets to identify shared features among the observations. By doing so, the two models continuously update each other and prevent overfitting, ultimately resulting in improved performance and robust generalization. Experimenting with synthetic data from the GALEX, SDSS, and HST surveys, we've demonstrated that our method surpasses traditional, specialist-demanded learning models in predicting object labels.

High-performance Arithmetic Coding (PAC Codes) are the standard method for lossless data compression in high-performance computing (HPC) storage.
Traditional compression approaches are largely ineffective on HPC data due to their inability to take into account the intricate structure of the data.
Recent research has demonstrated that next-generation codes, specifically supercodes of PAC Codes, can efficiently compress data computed by popular HPC applications, thus minimizing the data's storage size and network transmission cost.
To build these supercodes, it is crucial to understand how codes split and combine, thus facilitating the development of adaptive compression methods that adapt to changing data patterns during runtime.
To this end, we introduce a novel measurement of code splitting, enabling the dynamic reorganization of supercodes to optimize compression efficiency.
We further introduce a new algorithm for computing supercodes on the fly while a program executes, thus enabling real-time adaptation to changing data patterns in real-time.
Our method results in an n-fold reduction in storage requirements and network transmission costs for four test applications, specifically roms, sw4dmc, turbosquid, and turbosquid2.

A hand-to-object engagement is a fundamental interaction that underpins a wide range of real-world applications, but it's notably absent from current state-of-the-art technology. To bridge this gap, we've developed a novel method that can track engagements in unstructured environments using depth sensor data. This approach employs a engagement detection network and a pointcloud-to-3D-SKELETON transformer, which work together to analyze individual time-series frames. By treating hand object engagements as temporal sequences of skeletal data, our method can accurately model their dynamics and optimize for corresponding 3D representations. Extensive testing on a large real-world dataset demonstrates that our method surpasses existing solutions and even achieves better results for single frame-based engagement detection. Moreover, our method's performance rivals that of specialized 3D hand tracking methods when evaluated on a dataset with corresponding ground truth.

This research achieves a complete computation of the interleaving numbers for dimension 4 rank 4 noncrystallographic artin-algebraic tail-triangle C-collectives. Specifically, the study shows that the feasible ranks in a dimension 4 setting are either 4, or else it can be reexpressed as a semisimple collective of combined rank 4. The research further pinpoints that the rank 4 collectives are essentially equivalent to those in the D4, B4, A4d, and G2xB2 photonuclear interactions.

A versatile and adaptable method is devised for training robots to accurately position themselves and calculate the location of their end-effectors without relying on explicit depth camera data. By leveraging a powerful neural network, robots can learn from basic, easily obtainable data such as the content of an image, resulting in accurate 2D and 3D pose predictions. Furthermore, our proposed framework's results demonstrate superior performance compared to the current best approaches and even surpasses human-level accuracy in estimating end-effector positions from image content.

This study investigates the problem of identifying treatment disruption, a concept where the effectiveness of a treatment is diminished or extinguished when another treatment is implemented. We introduce a novel interference framework, specifically the k-nearest-neighbors (k-NN) interference model, which simulates the  k-NN  interference by assigning a non-negative weight to each neighbor based on their relationship to the target individual. Under this model, we develop conditions necessary for valid identification of treatment disruption, demonstrating its feasibility in simple scenarios such as linear models and the k-NN classification model.

The neutrino emission from self-annihilating Dark Matter within Neutron Stars is being investigated, specifically focusing on the contribution of a pseudoscalar mediator. By using the dense matter Chiral Perturbation Theory to improve the calculation at lower momentum transfers, the neutrino emissivity in Neutron Star matter has been re-evaluated. This revised calculation is comparative to the standard perturbation theory, particularly showing substantial differences in the neutrino spectrum and production rate, particularly at lower momentum transfers. Notably, the improved calculation is in better alignment with existing mirror neutron star data, thereby offering hope for future Neutron Star observations to verify the nature of Dark Matter.

The ongoing CFIS survey at the University of Toronto's Bumppo astronomical observatory is uniquely positioned for conducting strong-lensing studies, thanks to its extensive $r$-band coverage of the Northern sky up to the third magnitude. By leveraging the survey's data, we developed a customized filter for the Serna package to optimize shape assessment, specifically designed for UNIONS/CFIS's data format. This pipeline employs the multi-component elliptical gaussian model to segment individual galaxies and calculate their orientation. Our research yields a notable 35% increase in relevant data points across the $r_{\rm gal} < 0.5$ lensing efficacy regime compared to the existing method. Utilizing the newly implemented pipeline, we conducted a preliminary weak-lensing study of the CFIS data and derived a combined mass map by averaging the results from two adjacent $45^\circ$ quadrants, covering the $20<h<70$ range of galaxy clusters. This allows us to observe the sum of these clusters' masses, as measured in grams, across a $20.5\times20.5$ arcmin area of their central regions.

We analyze the behavior of a specific transcendental function, $g(n,m,\theta)$, which arises from investigating the placement of points in the square $0 \leq m \leq n$ on the torus. By proving an equation related to this function, we establish estimates for the distance between $m$ and $n-m$, which in turn allows us to study the distribution of points in the triangle $m \leq n-m < 0$. Additionally, this investigation leads to the determination of minimal values for certain expressions involving algebraic numbers, which in turn enables the computation of novel equidistribution measures on the torus related to the Kronecker-Weyl problem.

We prove that for k-rational singularities on smooth local complete intersections, k-Du Bois property holds, resulting in k-rationality being equivalent to k-Du Bois. For k-Du Bois local complete intersections, we show equilibrium points are present and characterize k-Du Boisness via the absence of such points for certain related singularities. Furthermore, we establish that k-rationality is hereditary for quasigraded local complete intersections with k-Du Bois property, also holding for certain mixed types.

A rare type of quantum phase transition occurs in highly-neighboring spins in metals when exposed to varying external magnetic fields, resulting in unique behaviors linked to field-dependent spin waves. We investigated this phenomenon in an analysis of highly-neighbored spin metals, using advanced experimental tools to observe field-dependent behaviors, field-pulse measurements, and microscopic analyses of highly-neighbored spin waves. Our results reveal that these metals exhibit a unique type of quantum phase transition and also exhibit characteristics of highly-neighbored spin waves in other materials, suggesting that these metals can exhibit field-dependent behaviors of highly-neighbored spin waves and also undergo a unique type of quantum phase transition.

Researchers have suggested a new theory, known as the Axion-Still-Neutrino Dark Matter model, to explain three distinct phenomena: why neutrinos don't follow standard high-temperature behavior, why dark matter clusters form easily, and why the ratio of dark matter to ordinary matter in the universe is biased towards heavier sides. To resolve these issues, this theory introduces two types of quasiparticles, called "photon mode" and "fermion mode", which arise from interacting with a specific field called the Higgs field. Simulations indicate that, when these quasiparticles are considered, neutrino behavior aligns with thermal expectations, and that larger-scale systems exhibit non-thermal characteristics. Furthermore, this model predicts that, in any given system, if the ratio of dark matter to ordinary matter is biased towards heavier sides, it will also be biased towards lighter sides. To test this model, researchers propose examining the galaxy cluster MS 2139-020 to look for discrepancies between expected and actual matter distributions, which could be resolved by accounting for dark matter and ordinary matter contributions separately.

Quantum computing's potential for speed and efficiency supersedes traditional computing, yet current devices are plagued by noisy data recovery. To mitigate this issue, the concept of fault-tolerant stabilizer code has been developed to effectively handle noisy data within these devices. To implement this code, it is crucial to determine the upper limits for the rank of qubits within these devices. Research has been conducted to establish an improved upper limit for the rank of magic states, an essential component of the fault-tolerant stabilizer code. The study also provides a theoretical underpinning for the existing bounds and introduces a novel analytical approach to establish the underpinning. The research further provides strengthened evidence linking the rank of magic states and the tolerance for multiple Pauli errors within these devices.

This research explores the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in four-dimensional Anti-de Sitter space, incorporating non-minimal quintessence field into the energy density term. The paper examines how this interaction impacts the optical properties of the model's holographic dark energy, using the quasi-static approach to derive a parameter-free function for the energy density, analyze its phase space, and calculate key cosmological parameters. The model is then analyzed under the quasi-static and fast-rolling conditions. The paper further discusses the difference between Tsallis and standard holographic dark energy in the phase space, before concluding with a discussion of the model's advantages.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopy Telescope (LAMOST) introduced a new functionality called the 'Time-Domain Observation' in 2020. This initiative enables repeated observations of select targets, allowing for the study of changing celestial objects. These targets are chosen from LAMOST's point source catalog based on exciting astronomical phenomena such as nova, supernova, and microlensing events. Four unique fields, each referred to as a 'K2 plate,' were observed as part of a larger project to explore varying sky phenomena. These four plates identified 375 unique targets across 1.63 square degrees, and through comparing these to the Hipparcos catalog, it became clear that many of these targets are primarily located close to the Sun. However, the plates also detected 54 blazar and 32 BL Lacertae candidates due to their bright optical emission. These findings serve as a starting point, and future targets have been selected with the intention of capturing key astronomical events including microlensing, nova, and supernova occurrences.

Previous research introduced the concept of truly random numbers generated from SRAM latency, 
which was later found to be flawed because it was predictable. Despite this flaw, the idea of 
generating random numbers by limiting SRAM latency to a predetermined minimum has merit. 
Therefore, a method called TuRaN has been developed to guarantee randomness by adjusting 
the voltage supplied to SRAM based on a minimum latency requirement. 
It is demonstrated that generating random numbers using TuRaN is faster and consumes less energy 
than current methods, while also being secure against analytical attacks.

A reliable and efficient method is devised for guiding a charge between specific molecular components using electrical impulses of varying duration. Initially, a set of molecular structures, referred to as single-electron resistive relays (ERRs), are computationally designed based on a sizeable number of existing molecular devices. Through extensive simulations of the electrical properties of these compounds, it's discovered that those with high electrical charges can effectively operate as relays while withstanding intense electrical signals. Ultimately, properties of four exemplary ERRs are analyzed and it's found that they possess the capacity to store electrical charges over extended periods and transmit these charges at rapid speeds, averaging 10 microseconds or faster.

We utilize modern central server technology to execute massless scalar 3-loop integrals in a fully symbolic and algebraic manner, leveraging color-dependent integral depictions as our primary tool of analysis. Our study covers a diverse range of 20 different parameters, some of which include 4-loop integrals derived from 3-loop integrals with internal dependencies, along with 2-loop integrals derived from scalar products. Our central server is designed with processing units that require minimal special instructions to execute complex algebra and polynomials, making it capable of handling high-level mathematical operations to produce the casework depictions directly. To streamline the evaluation process, we break down complex 4-loop parameters into a simplified form by separating off mass-dependent parts, then using a set of 2-loop parameters to derive these off-shell extensions. Our study includes a detailed comparison with published results using different methods, along with a dedicated section that provides a comprehensive review of our central server's functionality and a publicly accessible database of the casework depictions it produces.

We derive an expression to determine the basis eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional two-state quantum stride problem, where we consider a complex lattice structure consisting of two distinct sites separated by a jump step. These eigenfunctions are calculated using a novel formula, which reveals that it is possible to extend the eigenfunctions of the non-extending quantum stride model to those of the extending model, provided the tunneling rate between sites is sufficiently high. Additionally, our results indicate that certain degenerate states emerge in the extending model due to its lack of symmetry, which can be attributed to its wavefunction's non-orthogonality. These degenerate states can be decoupled through a unitary transformation, resulting in the desired basis eigenfunctions of the extending model. Finally, our findings are corroborated by numerical verification of the predicted eigenenergies and eigenfunctions.

Within the framework of the combined sigma-omega-rho paradigm combined with the vector meson dominance theory, we investigate the possibility of hybrid baryon mass generation as a function of various parameters within the framework of the combined sigma-omega-rho-jet quark and instanton models. We focus on calculating the mass of the delta and the nucleon and analyze their compactness and quark separation properties within the framework of the combined sigma-omega-rho-jet quark and instanton models.

This study examines the optical properties of a bi-mode $q$-deformed optomechanical system, focusing on the behavior of light in the context of transparency and amplification. By applying the ANO transform and analyzing the Fano resonances, we investigate how changes in time and phase affect the system's optical transmission and amplification. Additionally, we explore the impact of Sidhu-Liu convergence on the system's optical behavior. Our research further elucides how Debye asymptotics can optimize the $q$-deformed optomechanical system's transparency and amplification capabilities, influenced by the $|q|$ value.

In certain supersymmetric theories, specific types of compact stars experience an unusual phenomenon where their density increases unexpectedly at the center, resulting in unique and complex patterns of gravitational waves during supernova events. Researchers have found that these "scissors mode" signatures can be identified through precise analysis of a supernova's gravitational wave spectrum. They have determined that double rotators, characterized by interconnected rotation periods, can also exhibit "scissors mode" patterns, regardless of their mass and composition. Additionally, they discovered that R-parity violating theories can predict the suppression of "scissors mode" oscillations in certain fundamental frequencies, which can be confirmed by analyzing the shape of the star's global rotation pattern. If such theories are R-parity conserving, these oscillations should occur without restriction. Fundamental properties of these supersymmetric theories can be discerned by comparing the predicted "scissors mode" oscillations with actual data from supernova events and their accompanying gravitational waves. Researchers have made an initial estimation of a specific R-parity limiting parameter in these theories, suggesting a value of approximately 10^6 GeV. Further investigation of supernova events can provide more precise limitations on this parameter. Researchers have also found that these "scissors mode" oscillations can be detected by analyzing the 1608 s rotation pattern in the PSR B1633-47 pulsar, which can be attributed to a double rotator or a compact star with specific mass and composition. If these oscillations can be detected in

We examine the sublattice rotations and tilts in nanostructured metal-insulator structures, uncovering new physics and clarifying existing concepts through computer simulations. We begin by revisiting the polar metal-insulator phase and demonstrating how sublattice rotation and orbitals impact the resulting phase. We then explore the formation of a superdomain wall between adjacent domains with different rotations, identifying orbital degrees of freedom within the wall and their potential to act as a quantum battery. We also investigate the fusion of two domains with different rotations and find that their combination results in a larger, more complex structure with new properties. Finally, we examine the influence of external electric fields on these rotated layers and find that tilting of orbitals can either hinder or facilitate polarization levels, depending on the insulator material and its molecular structure.

Recent findings have revealed that ultracold gases can deviate from traditional statistical models when interacting with structured light, leading to peculiar correlations and distributions. Building on these discoveries, we have discovered novel, dissipative effects that occur when laser-cooled particles interact with complex optical patterns, resulting in unusual distributions and statistics not seen in non-dissipative situations. Specifically, our research shows that particles cooled to a state of equilibrium can exhibit unusual, non-Gaussian distributions characterized by negative correlations, as well as unusual statistics such as bimodality and higher moments of asymmetry. By employing optical grids as an example of complex light structures, our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the unusual statistics of particles in these situations, and suggests that particles exhibiting such behavior could serve as indicators of dissipation and enhance our understanding of this phenomenon.

This study examines the higher-order network properties of the cryptocurrency trading network, comprising a complex system driven by the interactions of individual traders, institutions, and automated trading tools. The research networks were constructed by tracing a link between entities that arises from one transaction affecting another, specifically through the transfer of funds. The analysis reveals a non-stationary pattern in the network's degree distribution, with the prevalence of short paths facilitating information and influence spread. The research also identifies a significant correlation between trading volume and node weights, suggesting the impact of institutional investment on the cryptocurrency trading network. The results were sustained using data from multiple periods. The research implies that to gain a deeper understanding of the cryptocurrency trading dynamics, it's necessary to focus on both the individual actions and the collective behavior of traders, aided by analysis of the resulting networks.

The formation of particles that can lead to atmospheric cloud formation is influenced by the association of water and sulfuric acid molecules. The thermal energy caused by zero-point motion has the potential to impact this process at its earliest stages. Using simulations based on path-integrated ab initio molecular dynamics (AI-PMI), the role of zero-point energy was examined in the early stages of growth of sulfuric acid-water clusters. The results show that it often enables the formation of larger, more stable structures than would be possible at equilibrium temperatures. The findings indicate a significant positive effect of zero-point energy on the formation of particles in this system.

We establish the closure of the set of operator awareness pairs $(T,S)$ with $T$ quasi-invertible, and investigate the compactness of the space of group equivariant non-dilating operators on $H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$.

The thermal Hall effect in a quantum anomaly can be compared to its gravitational counterpart, which occurs in the vicinity of an extremal, rotating black hole. However, there are some key differences between these two phenomena. Specifically, the thermal Hall effect does not adhere to the conventional Einstein relations when considered in the context of a quantum anomaly, which has significant implications for understanding the local dynamics of this phenomenon. Furthermore, we have observed that the thermal Hall effect does not follow the anticipated scaling behavior of its gravitational counterpart, which may have far-reaching consequences for hypothesizing dual descriptions of these two phenomena.

We examine how complex neural networks' solutions are regulated by various factors, which vary depending on the data and network complexity. To understand this, we developed a novel loss function, combining data-specific simplification and generalization capabilities. This framework, Neural Simplification Barriers (NSB), explains several phenomena: overfitting, underfitting, feature extraction, generalization, neural network complexity, and the effectiveness of various regularization techniques. By reformulating NSB into an optimization problem with a predictable solution, we demonstrate that a form of NSB is optimized during neural network training, and its solutions are simpler than those without this regularization. Furthermore, we show that the number of layers in a neural network is an implementation detail, influencing solution complexity. We also discuss the connections to prior research in dynamical systems and the limitations of simplicity in neural networks.

We suggest a strategy to determine the Wilson coefficients of New Physics influences in rare $B$ meson decays, specifically using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays with fully-leptonic final states. By utilizing flavor theory and input from $B^0\to K^{*0}\gamma$ and $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$(with a lepton pair) decays, we can precisely calculate one coefficient, thereby reducing uncertainty in the others by a factor of four, ultimately allowing for Wilson coefficient determination with an accuracy of $2\%$ in the standard model. This approach also enables the identification of New Physics influences with confidence levels exceeding $90\%$.

When assessing the completeness and coherence of generated text, standard metrics such as BLEU and Ngram Coverage fall short.
We've investigated several strategies to strengthen these metrics by incorporating additional information about the reference texts.
We've discovered that a pre-trained textual transformer model can efficiently process the enhanced input to produce a more accurate output.
Furthermore, our research has identified a method to combine multiple enhanced inputs in a transformer framework, outperforming previous metrics and state-of-the-art composition evaluation methods in several cases.

This article develops a comprehensive framework for measuring and analyzing the concept of marginal dependence between two random variables, X and Y. The framework consists of a fundamental definition and various methodologies to assess this dependence, which are further discussed in terms of their practical applications and theoretical implications. By considering the marginal distribution of X and Y, our framework can identify and evaluate the impact of dependence on statistical models, functional relationships, and random variables, as seen in the discussion of copula models. Specifically, we examine the link between marginal dependence measures and their relationship with the underlying distribution's characteristics, such as skewness and kurtosis, as well as their connection to the more widely recognized concept of dependence measured by the correlation coefficient.

We develop a model of human capital formation to analyze the passage of opportunities from one generation to the next, incorporating elements of uncertainty and conflict through the concept of a 'prospect landscape'. This framework is inspired by Sovereign's theory of social mobility and we adapt it to prioritize the distribution of these 'prospect' opportunities, representing paths to success, among a population over a finite time horizon. A prospect landscape is a graphical representation of these opportunities and we introduce two measures, average height and mean width, to quantify the distribution of these prospects among a population over a finite time period. Both measures are meaningful solutions to a optimization problem distributing prospects to maximize the expected value of these opportunities, a concept rooted in Fubini's theorem. We then demonstrate the existence of unique and stationary algebras under two specific conditions, the presence of an endogenous conflict and a predictable sequence of events.

The spin-statistics connection relies on the application of the commutation or anticommutation relationship of the components of the Pauli matrices. This paper reexamines this link by focusing solely on the parity of the wave functions, which results in the same proof of the Pauli principle. It is demonstrated that the proof of the spin-statistics theorem can be based on the parity of the wave functions without relying on the commutators of the spin operators.

We introduce an upgraded version of RingCT with enhanced performance, allowing for increased transaction processing on the Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS) blockchain. The revised RingCT, dubbed 'Delegated RingCT,' integrates the computationally efficient Ring Signature type 'Ring Sylvester' to maintain the principles of anonymity, linkability, and unlinkability while significantly reducing processing time. The Delegated RingCT design involves the separation of public keys and secret keys, enabling a delegate's Secret Key Authority to sign transactions anonymously on behalf of users with public keys, thus improving transaction speed and efficiency.

We examine the space complexity of downstream tasks driven by linear algebra, specifically focusing on the worst-case scenario of solving general linear equations, for which the best-known space complexity bound is O~(n^3.3073), obtained by following Strassen's divide-and-conquer matrix multiplication algorithm. We show that this space complexity is achievable in the context of 2D tensor contraction, and that a significant portion of existing work in tensor contraction is comprised of algorithms that have a space complexity of O~(n^1.6152), essentially equivalent to solving linear equations.
