Two distinct methods were employed to measure J/psi production: one used the electron-positron continuum in the same collisions for normalization and another used a bottom-up approach to directly calculate production rates. Both methods agreed on the J/psi differential cross-section at midrapidity. This measurement is compared with theoretical models, such as the EPPS1 and EPPS2 phenomenological models, which predicted J/psi production based on nuclear parton distribution functions.

We've developed and tested an advanced system for creating audio responses to visual stimuli. The system employs a neural network that integrates information from both visual and auditory sources, allowing it to produce high-quality audio adapted to the visual input. Key aspects of our method involve a novel approach to combining visual features, establishing a link between visual inputs and auditory styles, and utilizing pre-trained models to achieve seamless audio production. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our system surpasses a comparison model in producing audio that's visually guided and of superior quality.

Epistemic uncertainty in machine learning can be monitored by using ensemble methods that gauge the diversity of predictions made at the prediction time. However, current techniques are limited in their ability to grasp complex temporal structures due to the assumption of independent prediction variability. This assumption is not valid for time series data, leading to inaccurate measures of uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel approach utilizing recurrent neural networks is presented to acquire sequential information regarding data variance for enhanced uncertainty assessment. The proposed method is flexible, adaptable to various task types (regression and classification), and outperforms established benchmarks in the field of uncertainty estimation.

Achieving a balance between minimizing epidemic-related deaths and economic losses requires timely epidemic countermeasures.  We show that when the number of dead and economic losses are represented by quadratic functions, the optimal policy involves implementing the same countermeasure level in all regions.  Additionally, the optimal strategy is to switch countermeasures only when the epidemic reaches a specific threshold, which is calculated based on average regional characteristics.  Finally, both the number of dead and economic losses decrease in a predictable, exponential pattern as the countermeasure level increases.

This study addresses a key problem in machine learning by pinpointing data issues
arising during model training. To accomplish this, we utilize the Shapley value to
assess the influence of each data item on model performance. Our proposed framework
consists of three modules that identify data problems, compute the Shapley value
for data items, and develop strategies to mitigate data issues for ongoing training.
Extensive experiments were conducted across various application scenarios, including
image classification, sentence translation, and video classification. The results show that
our framework effectively locates data problems and achieves high accuracy in
identifying the influence of data items. Additionally, it offers valuable insights to
guide model training and enhances model performance by addressing data problems.
Notably, the Shapley significance of data items revealed biases present in popular
computer vision datasets, shedding light on future research and development.

This study provides a detailed examination of the relationships between enumerative geometry and other areas of mathematics like combinatorics, probability theory, and topological invariant theory, while also exploring their connections to statistical mechanics and random matrix theory. We thoroughly investigate the implications of the duality principle, combining various mathematical concepts such as degree, multiplicity, dimension, and parity to derive meaningful relationships between these concepts in different branches of mathematics.

This study explores how high pressure influences the electronic and magnetic properties of Mn$_3$Sn, a well-studied triangular antiferromagnet with notable anomalous Hall effects. Using symmetry analysis and ab-initio calculations, researchers discovered that increasing pressure converts Mn$_3$Sn into a Heisenberg antiferromagnet at 170 kbar, accompanying a semimetal-to-metal phase transition. This trimerization phenomenon is predicted to occur in an exotic, recently identified spin-triplet topological state within Mn$_3$Sn at high pressure. Experimental data, including magnetization, resistivity, and anomalous Hall effect measurements, supports the existence of this new state. Notably, the results suggest that the trimerization state can be manipulated numerically through pressure to control the direction of the Hall effect, offering a novel pathway to utilize topological materials in functional technology.

Deep neural networks hold significant promise for automatically extracting relationships between entities in text. Research in this area has shown consistent improvements over the past eight years, with recent advances yielding high accuracy in relation extraction. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research in relation extraction using deep neural networks, covering topics such as input representation, supervised and semi-supervised learning methods, as well as the application of pre-trained language models.

This study centers around a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the dependence of this eigenvalue on the radius $r$ and how its derivative behaves at $r=0$, effectively studying a singular Steklov eigenvalue problem in this context.

We introduce the problem of guided hypergraph restoration, where the goal is to reconstruct a high-level representation of data from its compressed form across multiple dimensions, while incorporating prior knowledge about the relationships between these dimensions. Specifically, we aim to remove unnecessary compression in complex data sets, enabling better understanding and analysis of their inherent structures. Leveraging the properties of hypergraphs as frameworks for modeling these relationships, we develop an iterative algorithm that utilizes numerical optimization techniques to effectively restore the data and preserve the underlying graph structure. Our method is capable of handling missing and noisy values, and we demonstrate its efficacy through experiments on synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its performance and data-driven graph visualizations.

To advance radiologist training and improve automated diagnosis systems for chest X-rays, high-quality and diverse annotations are essential for dataset enhancement. However, creating these annotations is labor-intensive, limiting practical applications. To overcome this challenge, we developed an advanced system that enhances chest X-ray images using computed tomography (CT) projections, thereby expanding training data without requiring additional manual annotations. The system relies on cycle-generative adversarial networks (CGANs) trained on unlabelled CT scans and achieves notable improvements in performance, particularly in predicting findings and image modifications. The study showcases that extending X-ray training data with our method enhances performance, yielding superior results, and demonstrates potential for enhancing radiologist decision-making skills and contributing to the development of accurate automated diagnosis systems.

We establish a key relationship between the Euler characteristics of certain space-forms and subspaces associated with tight contact manifolds, now linked to the Thurston norm. Our research also yields new insights into multi-grasp frameworks for hyperbolic manifolds. Additionally, we offer a revised definition of the Euler characteristic of a space-form, valid for any tight contact manifold, along with a characeterization involving the Thurston norm. This characterization leads to a conjecture regarding the upper bound of the Euler characteristic, now proven for frameworks comprising a single source and multiple sinks.

We investigated the entropic characteristics of microcavity laser systems that exhibit unidirectional emission. By analyzing the functional relationship between the entropy of the emitted intensity and the current injection current, we identified a pivotal role played by the spatial structure of the microcavity. Additionally, our findings revealed that in the stationary state, the entropy of the emitted intensity is insensitive to the spatial structure, whereas the dynamic behavior is heavily influenced by it. Furthermore, we explored how the statistical properties of current injection influence the entropic characteristics of the emitted intensity. Our research delves into the entropic properties of microcavity laser systems to gain insight into their complex directional emission phenomena.

The rising popularity of cryptocurrencies, driven by their 'decentralized' nature, has sparked debate over their potential to replace traditional currencies. As a key aspect, we examine whether the cost consistency of cryptocurrencies, particularly in a context of infinite supply, enables them to serve as a reliable medium of exchange. Building on a cost model developed by Scharfstein (2014), we demonstrate that, under specific conditions, a cryptocurrency maintaining a positive equilibrium price with a finite number of holders would require an infinitely large number of holders. This outcome is consistent with the findings of earlier research (Krause et al. (2017), Green and Knight (2011-12)) that, in a 2-player setting, cryptocurrencies are not viable for exchange purposes.

By integrating inverse scattering, nonlinear Schrödinger equation, Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation, faint noise, and out-of-equilibrium thermodynamics within a unified framework, we demonstrate that the reverse scattering framework offers a straightforward method for analyzing non-equilibrium systems, thereby bridging the gap between integrable models and general thermodynamic systems.

To understand how the solar breeze's compressive turbulence affects its protons, we analyzed data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission, focusing on events with high spacecraft potentials. These potentials indicate the energetic electrons' proximity to the spacecraft. We observed that, in most cases, the turbulence's large-scale properties remained consistent regardless of the electrons' position, but the details of the turbulence's small scales varied significantly. Our findings suggest that the turbulence's very small scales (less than 10 electron scales) are influenced by the electrons' presence. We based our analysis on both visual inspections and statistical evaluations of the data. These results have important implications for future solar breeze observations, suggesting the use of multiple probes at the shock and in the downstream area to capture complete and unbiased data. Additionally, the data indicate the presence of two distinct types of turbulence at the shock, with one exhibiting directional dependence and the other not.

In SASE FEL schemes, achieving high average power requires generating as many as tens of megawatts of electromagnetic radiation in extremely short durations, typically on the order of few hundred attoseconds. Conventional gap-based undulators often experience charge-related hindrances that limit their maximum average power capabilities, typically in the range of kilowatts. To overcome this constraint, researchers have explored alternative schemes such as self-seeding, shared-source SASE, and hollow undulators. However, the latter two methods have associated trade-offs in terms of cost, operational complexity, and feasibility. To address this challenge, we have been working on establishing a modified charge-taper scheme for generating high-power attosecond bursts using third-generation FEL facilities. This method involves utilizing a natural separation between charge and current in an undulator to produce a natural gap, thereby enabling the production of high-power attosecond bursts without added complexity or trade-offs. We have successfully implemented this approach at the FLASH facility to achieve tens of megawatts of XUV and soft X-ray radiation with high peak currents, enabling the development of attosecond pulses with significant energy.

Field observations from the Namib Desert and laboratory experiments have shown that shear flows can be accurately predicted by analyzing dune field geometry, even in areas without detailed wind data. We have found that these flows display a common pattern in which a stable layer forms at the base of a sand dune. The top layer of this system is subject to turbulent forces, but remains largely influenced by the underlying current. We have developed a theoretical model to better understand and predict these flows. The model relies on detailed information about the dune field's shape and the properties of the layers in these systems. We have also created equations to describe the flow's velocity and direction, as well as methods to calculate key variables in these systems.

We propose a novel method to quantify gerrymandering by leveraging the principles of simulated tempering, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique. This approach allows us to explore the parameter space of a political district drawing algorithm, assessing its effectiveness through the use of multiple criteria, all while dynamically adjusting its temperature to enhance exploration. By employing a temperature schedule that prioritizes discovery over thoroughness, we can efficiently discover the political affiliations of voters in optimal draws, thereby valuing political influence in these districts. A fully automated system, incorporating both the simulated tempering algorithm and a K-means clustering method to determine affiliation thresholds, can objectively measure gerrymandering by focusing on the political balance of a district's voters.

Textile authentication is crucial in ensuring the integrity of textile products. For efficient identification of forgeries in textured images, we've developed a novel flaw detection method that combines Gabor wavelet energy gradient (GHOG) and low-rank decomposition. Firstly, GHOG is applied to extract features from an authenticated textile image, and then a low-rank nonconvex proximal point algorithm is employed to minimize rank deficiency and data discrepancy in a suspect textile image. The results demonstrate that our method effectively detects flaws and verifies the authenticity of textile products.

To successfully navigate a visual environment, a model must balance two key considerations. On one hand, the agent needs to take effective actions that reduce the discrepancy between its current observation and the desired goal. On the other hand, the model must achieve this goal while adhering to a reasonable trajectory of observations, preventing the model from generating misleading scenarios with invalid sightlines. Regulating the flow of observations is particularly crucial when working with real-world datasets that may contain diverse scenarios. Existing methods have made progress but have failed to fully address the issue, largely due to a lack of explicit model constraints. To bridge this gap, our research proposes the Image Consistency Loss, which enforces a model to produce coherent sightlines and helps the reinforcement learning agent achieve better results. To achieve this, our method derives the ICL from the data-theoretic perspective of the relative entropy between navigational states, and it is shown to be effective in promoting various beneficial traits, including image consistency, navigational coherence, and predictive capability, all while minimizing data regularization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses comparable methods by a significant margin and achieves notable success in navigating complex environments with real-world images and challenging scenarios.

Investigating near-black-hole formations through simulations of collapsing star clusters reveals a crucial aspect influencing their outcome. Specifically, a near-black-hole's growth rate determines whether the emerging black hole's mass falls within anticipated range or exceeds it substantially. Previous studies demonstrated that a key factor determining this growth rate is the rate at which a near black hole's mass decreases, specifically its loss rate. This study focuses on this loss rate by analyzing simulations of star cluster collapses. It compares the loss rates from simulations involving near-black-hole formations and those without such formations. The goal is to establish a benchmark for this loss rate to guide future simulations and modeling efforts.

We examine the formation of the initial stellar mass function in dense nuclear star clusters and its later evolution to account for the lack of massive stars observed today. Using population synthesis, we find that this absence is consistent with a mass range of early star formation being concentrated in high-mass stars, typically ranging from 10 to 100 times the mass of our sun. These high-mass stars would have left behind dense objects like black holes and neutron stars, which would have formed in the early stages of star cluster evolution. Furthermore, the mergers of these dense objects within the star cluster would have generated significant gravitational waves in the early universe, particularly in the low-frequency range that is not detectable by LIGO. We predict a more substantial number of these undetectable mergers at higher star masses, and the pattern of these mergers is consistent with the overall trend of star formation observed in the universe.

In modern high-tech communities, reliable monitoring of substation and feeder equipment in power distribution networks is a pressing need. Current monitoring methods are primarily based on online device information reports, which are inadequate due to the limited data they can collect and the difficulties they pose for data analysis. To address these challenges, we've developed an advanced data analysis system that can extract valuable insights from vast amounts of installation and operation data, including event logs, maintenance records, and wisdom gathered from years of operational experience. This system can identify incidents of unusual behavior, pinpoint the source of the issue, and provide critical data for troubleshooting and diagnostic purposes. To validate the effectiveness of this system, we analyzed the actual data from a actual power distribution network, using machine learning algorithms to compare its performance against the current standard method and a control group with no identified events. The results show that our approach significantly outperforms the existing method in accurately detecting events and reducing false positives.

Our study focuses on examining $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi$ decays using an effective field theory relevant to spin-1 heavy quarkonia physics. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi$ decays are further analyzed under different $X(3872)$ interpretations. The $X(3872)$ is assumed to have a $1^{+}$ quantum state, and all form factors are derived mathematically. The obtained results for the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\gamma$ process include a detailed prescription for determining the differential photon spectrum, in addition to total decay widths. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi$ decays are broken down into $\pi^0, \pi^\pm$ components, with the $\pi^\pm$ decay mode split into $J/\psi \pi^\pm$ and $\gamma \pi^\pm$ modes. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi$ decay widths for different $X(3872)$ interpretations and quarkonia states are compared, with our study's findings ultimately presented in a summary table for both decays.

We provide a comprehensive description of quadric surfaces within the context of 3-dimensional projective geometry, emphasizing its categorical formulation. This approach describes quadrics through their association with self-dual mutations of Gorenstein algebras, thereby offering a comprehensive understanding of their linear series and line configurations. Additionally, this framework allows us to classify line configurations of quadrics, resulting in a comprehensive enumeration of their varieties.

We introduced TextWorldExpress, a groundbreaking text-based game engine built on C++, designed for rapid development and unparalleled speed - capable of processing over one million moves per second, making it the most high-performance platform of its kind. TextWorldExpress outperforms its popular alternative, TextWorld, by a staggering factor of nearly 200 times, while also offering a user-friendly interface and an extensive library of features and tools. Our engine boasts sophisticated AI capabilities, sophisticated search algorithms and a wealth of educational resources, as well as a thriving community of researchers and students. Our benchmark tests reveal that TextWorldExpress achieves incredible speeds on diverse hardware, averaging 226,000 moves per second on a basic laptop and 1,017,000 moves per second on a top-of-the-range gaming PC. Our benchmark results also reveal impressive acceleration factors of up to 42 times and 195 times, respectively. TextWorldExpress truly pushes the boundaries of text-based game simulation, paving the way for groundbreaking applications and research.

We develop a method to study topological insulators with defects using A-geometric methods, which treat defects as A-connections. Our approach, akin to Connes' study of connections on spin manifolds, allows us to define spectral invariants for the flux of topological insulators with defects. These invariants, derived from the Pimsler-Voiculescu transformation, quantify the flux's spectral properties and its impact on the physical system. Notably, our method permits the extension of topological insulators with defects to include diverse flux types, such as non-trivial band flux and dynamical flux associated with Chern-Simons functions. Furthermore, our framework enables the generalization of spectral invariants to the B-connection of the Floquet system, offering new insights into the dynamics of topological insulators with defects.

This research delves into a variety of $p$-harmonic functions within two-dimensional sectors, focusing on their classification, growth rates, and mean value property. Our work builds on existing knowledge from the literature to provide new insights and connections to mean concave and concave functions.

Significant wind-driven flooding is a burgeoning issue for communities in coastal areas, necessitating a deeper understanding of extreme weather phenomena to pinpoint high-risk locations and develop effective mitigation strategies.

Current methods for identifying extreme weather events are primarily grounded in univariate approaches, overlooking the intricate relationships between multiple environmental factors that contribute to flooding.

This research introduces a multivariate spatial model to analyze and visualize the correlation between coastal flooding and environmental conditions, utilizing a Bayesian Gaussian Mixture framework to segment the study area into distinct regions with shared statistical characteristics.

The proposed model is applied to a real-world dataset from Newfoundland's marine environment, generating maps that illustrate the probability of extreme weather conditions within specific areas based on the local wind and wave conditions.

These maps can inform coastal hazard assessments, inform residents about their vulnerability to flooding, and guide local authorities in adapting to these emerging events.

We establish that for a number field $K$, the set of non-constant polynomial functions from $K$ to $K$ is finite. Furthermore, this finding has been generalized to the set of non-constant rational functions from $K$ to $K$, and the results have also been proven for the corresponding sets of phi-functions and psi-functions.

A key concept called manipulability realm adjustment, specifically for rigid bodies in 3D space, is addressed. It Involves calculating the most suitable orientation of an object relative to a grasp position, considering only graspable positions without accounting for a grasp's specifics. This paper proposes a new method, using parallel conveyance and a manifold-aware Iterative Closest Point algorithm, to refine existing adjustement approaches. Experimental results validate the proposed method's efficacy in making manipulability realm adjustments for spheres, cylinders, and cubes using kinematic data from a real robotic arm setup.

In a study to evaluate Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process at the LHC, the matrix element method serves as the primary technique to differentiate signal from background. Although the massive vector boson pair production process via a gluon fusion is the dominant source of Higgs boson pairs, top quark pairing remains a supplementary production mechanism. This research investigates how effective the matrix element method is in the top quark pairing channel by comparing it to simulated data. Additionally, we examine if combining the matrix element method with other techniques such as neural networks and ScotCat can enhance the process's sensitivity to Higgs boson pair detection.

Turntables 3D object database, widely used for 3D object rendering research, has been found to contain images taken at angles that are not part of the original rotation cadence. As a result, when these additional views are combined with the existing ones, the pose estimation models can achieve nearly perfect performance without being explicitly programmed for it. This phenomenon is referred to as unintentional turntables and can be seen as a form of transfer learning, where the models gain skills from these extra views and apply them to new situations. However, if the views not part of the original cadence were to be removed, the models would struggle, relying instead on low-quality 3D object renderings that actually do contain the relevant information but are of lower quality.

The rapid spread of misinformation through social media about the COVID-19 pandemic has led to severe consequences, while interactive platforms like Twitter can facilitate counter-measures to combat this issue. We have developed an innovative framework to pinpoint instances of misinformation dissemination on Twitter regarding COVID-19 vaccines in conversations. The proposed framework combines specific technical features and human assessments as a baseline to distinguish acceptance from rejection of such misinformation. We have also derived a novel set of technical indicators capable of matching human-identified indicators of acceptance and refusal of misinformation with considerable precision. The integration of these technical features and human assessments enables the identification of refusal of misinformation with a high level of accuracy, outperforming the human-based approach in certain instances.

Recent breakthroughs have made it possible to generate high-energy attosecond pulses in the hard X-ray range using advanced laser technology. Despite the extremely short duration of these pulses, typically measured in fractions of an attosecond, their coherent manipulation poses a significant technical challenge due to the intricate quantum interplay between pulses and atoms. In this study, we successfully address this limitation by developing a novel scheme for isolating and enhancing attosecond pulses in the presence of strong fields. Our findings predict the creation of a robust, field-resistant attosecond pulse with 7.2 attosecond duration at a wavelength of 12.7 nm, achievable using 40 fs laser pulses and a gas mixture of N$_2$ and Ar. This proposed method has the potential to serve as a foundational technique for the coherent manipulation of ultrashort pulses, enabling the exploration of extreme non-equilibrium physics and the development of next-generation light sources.

Recent discoveries using direct imaging and high-contrast mapping techniques have led to the revision of the binary system for the traditional stellar example ALF Tau AB. By analyzing spatial and temporal properties captured through high-resolution imaging and spectroscopic observations, a team of researchers re-examined the evidence for the revised binary system and confirmed the existence of a third component in a highly eccentric orbit with a relatively short period. Further analysis indicated that this third component, initially thought to be a planet, actually meets the criteria for a companion stellar object, referred to as a T dissociation object, and exhibits characteristics distinct from those of known brown dwarfs and planets in the ALF Tau system.

This study focuses on solving the nonlinear Schrödinger equation under the condition u<sub>tt</sub> = Δu + |u|<sup>p-1</sup> u in a bounded area of R<sup>d</sup>, with d is greater than or equal to 2, outside a smooth convex obstacle. We prove that for a specified initial data with p greater than or equal to 1 + 4/d, the equation has an explosive solution that occurs at a specific time when the L<sup>∞</sup> norm of the initial data is large enough.

In recent years, Physics-Informed Neural Networks have gained significant traction as a means to solve partial differential equations with consideration to physical laws. Despite the robustness of PINNs on a wide array of PDEs, they often fall short in covering the entire solution space, particularly in cases with sharp solutions. To mitigate this, enhancing the solution precision requires a precise grid, which in the context of PINNs, translates to adapting the node distribution based on the residual behavior. To address this challenge, we present RANG, a flexible and efficient adaptive node creation technique revolving around residual-based node creation, featuring both global and local creation components that account for overall solution quality and localized irregularities. Empirical results on various test cases reveal RANG's superiority over comparable methods in terms of solution precision and diversity.

This study examines the behavior of a multi-domain ferroelectric FET, specifically its gate tunneling current, to understand how varying the thickness of the channel and insulator layers affects its operation. A custom-built simulation tool is used to replicate domain behavior, accurate to the nanoscale, and validate these results against existing experimental data. Furthermore, a mathematical model is developed to simulate a negative capacitance effect, which is also validated against experimental data. A comprehensive analysis of the device's physical properties, including its energy band, charge states, and electrostatic potential, is also provided.

The increasing complexity of freight systems across the globe drives up the demand for freight services, emphasizing the need to measure the resilience of freight networks. This study focuses on freight ecosystems as a framework for analyzing and improving freight system resilience. Using a United States-based freight system as a case study, we created a dependency-fragility insight graph to assess the resilience of freight-bounded supply chains. We then evaluated the effect of freight disruptions on supply chain costs, considering the interdependence of freight, inventory, and customer demands. Our research found that freight disruptions can lead to increased inventory holding costs in supply chains, and freight vulnerabilities are spread to affected regions through supply chains, resulting in elevated costs for these areas.

This study examines the irreducibility of stochastic Ginzburg-Landau equations affected by pure jump disturbances and demonstrates their equivalent impact to a single location pure jump disturbance plus a white noise disturbance in terms of irreducibility. Additionally, the research illustrates the irreducibility of these stochastic equations in two distinct scenarios: with a single location pure jump disturbance and in the absence of noise, utilizing the L\'evy rotation method.

For each prime number $p$, we explore the lowest possible value of the degree of the power graph associated with a finite $p$-group of a particular size. Our investigation leads to several effective findings regarding the least degree of power graphs for finite $p$-groups. Specifically, we've successfully determined the minimum degree for a given group order in numerous instances, provided a criterion for achieving the minimum degree, and established a lower bound for the minimum degree in general cases. Additionally, our research yields a straightforward proof that power graphs of finite nilpotent groups are perfect.

TAAS (TASC-Auger Spectrometer) is a cutting-edge hadron spectrometer designed to operate at the LHC and TAAS (Tenerife Air Shower) observatory on the J-PET-like principle. TAAS aims to optimize energy performance for reconstructing hadron interaction patterns in the forward region of the LHC and explore novel methods to identify cosmic air showers via the decay of neutral hadrons into X-rays, utilizing the Earth's surface as a massive detector for low-energy photons. TAAS features a unique, portable, and compact architecture with high sensitivity, encompassing an array of 40 times greater magnitude over a broad energy range of 10 GeV to 10 TeV. This innovative system incorporates a double-layer micromesh detector, a tracking chamber with magnetic field, a shashlik calorimeter, an electromagnetic calorimeter, and a tail catcher with Cherenkov detectors. TAAS utilizes the LHC to test detector performance in high-luminosity environments and the TAAS to investigate cosmic-ray physics by detecting secondary X-rays produced by the decay of neutral hadrons and primary photons within the cosmic air showers.

Deep learning techniques have become popular again due to their ability to effectively tackle complex problems, specifically focusing on the topic of image classification. In recent years, researchers have revived various outdated models and modified them to fit modern convolutional networks. This study aims to enhance the performance of these networks by incorporating orientation-sensitive layers, resulting in a more accurate classification rate for the CIFAR-10 dataset. Moreover, we introduce a novel architecture, called the Orientation Convolutional Network (OCN), which combines the benefits of both convolutional and orientation-sensitive layers. Our experiments demonstrate that the OCN outperforms other structures, achieving a competitive result of 86.91% accuracy for the CIFAR-10 dataset.

This study seeks to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of point cloud processing tasks, specifically classification and segmentation. In point cloud classification, we aim to accurately identify the geometric features of point clouds to achieve superior results. In the context of point cloud segmentation, we strive to effectively extract and localize individual point cloud features. Building on the effectiveness of graph convolutional networks (GCNs), we introduce a novel GCN framework tailored for point cloud processing. This method distinguishes itself from existing approaches with its repeated graph convolutional operations, which facilitate data extraction from complex point cloud structures. Moreover, we have carefully designed and optimized the key components of our framework, including the node feature, affinity matrix, and weight matrix to yield optimal results. The empirical outcomes validate the effectiveness of our proposed solution.

We introduce a groundbreaking form of trojan attacks titled Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault (SHTA), allowing for undetectable backdoors in deep learning models without requiring host gradient modification. Building on the concept of HTA, SHTA can be categorized into two types: backdoor client and backdoor trigger. In experiments, we specifically targeted image classification tasks and validated the effectiveness of our approach by achieving a minimal loss in accuracy while ensuring that the model's parameters and activation maps remain unchanged. Furthermore, our proposed method has been successfully tested on various image classification models and against multiple defense strategies, showcasing its efficacy and versatility.

Introduced in 2016, the Magellan-IMACS Wide-field Integral Field Device (MWIFD) is an upgrade to the IMACS spectrograph on the 2.8m Leonhard Schmadel telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. This paper details the enhancements and refinements made to the MWIFD's design and software between its initial implementation and the present. A comprehensive overview of the system's features and performance is also provided. Specifically, the upgrades addressed initial limitations of the IFD's optics, optimized its performance across its 4.67 field of view, and resolved issues related to the device's controller and data processing complexities. Enhanced performance includes a 50% increase in spatial resolution, improved spectral coverage, and increased spatial sampling. These improvements and refinements position the MWIFD as a highly capable instrument for a range of scientific applications, including galaxy evolution studies, emission-line object surveys, and atmospheric wind research.

We examine the ongoing progress of the Trojan horse technique in combining data from sub-coulomb particle scattering and high-energy transfer reactions to analyze composite particle formation. Specifically, we focus on the advancement in understanding the deep sub-coulomb region of the $^{12}$C + $^{12}$C scattering cross-section and its significance in evaluating the $^{12}$C + $^{12}$C fusion reaction at energy near the threshold. Additionally, we emphasize the potential of the Trojan horse technique in resolving long-standing issues related to pre-compilation electron scattering data and in uncovering hidden reaction channels through an inverse reaction approach.

A crucial factor determining the formation and construction of terrestrial-type exoplanets' cores is the type of core that forms in their host stars. Studying the core characteristics in host stars is therefore of high importance. We have developed an expanded model to investigate core characteristics by applying a mixed-core ADK (MC-ADK) model, which combines features of homogenous cores and heterogeneous cores. By utilizing this model, we analyzed 21 stars hosting terrestrial-type planets, and discovered that 18 of these stars can be explained by the MC-ADK model. The core characteristics in these stars can vary significantly, ranging between 0.15 and 6.3 M$_{\odot}$. We also found that planets around low-metallicity stars typically have cores formed primarily through light elements, whereas in planets around metal-rich stars, the core composition is dominated by iron. Additionally, metal-rich stars tend to have core masses significantly larger than low-metallicity stars. This research laid the groundwork for MC-ADK models to be applied in future studies on exoplanetary systems.

In recent years, Wireless Sensing through CSI (Channel State Information) has become a preferred method for outdoor large-scale positioning due to its high accuracy, low cost, and coverage extension capabilities. However, the narrowbeams used in CSI technology can lead to partial visibility and reduced coverage, which hampers its effectiveness in position estimation. To address this limitation, this research proposes an advanced deep learning-based Wireless Sensing framework that leverages attention mechanisms to focus on critical angles and related CSI data, thereby maximizing coverage and position estimation accuracy. The framework's effectiveness is validated through comprehensive simulations and field experiments, which reveal significant performance gains over existing positioning methods utilizing narrowbeams.

This paper offers a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking its various sound and complete topological semantics in a unified categorical setting. The proposed framework is versatile and accommodates a range of topological categories that are relevant in philosophical logic, such as the categories for preorders, partial orders, and bisimilarity. Building on the structural composition method, we demonstrate how to obtain both sound and complete Kripke semantics and modal algebra semantics starting from the topological categories.

We are counteracting the concept of robust edge-tinted Hamiltonian partitions introduced in a previous study. A particular class of cubic bipartite graphs known as "cage graphs" serves as a counterexample, demonstrating that the previous study's key finding was flawed. We establish a revised theorem that is applicable to all cubic bipartite graphs, along with a computational method for determining whether a given graph complies with the revised theorem.

We examine the functions of n variables defined on the Hamming graphs, with the constraint that their spectral radius does not exceed $\sqrt{n}$. It is established that the lowest possible dimension of support for such functions is at least n, with the exception of affine functions which have a support dimension of n-k for k affine functions of n variables. Notably, this outcome contradicts earlier findings which showed that non-affine functions with a support dimension of n were abundant, with a c-fold excess for a suitable constant c.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-enabled interface that enables secure access to COPASI functions via a browser, allowing multiple users to run simulations and analyses simultaneously. We present a new framework for extending COPASI's functionality through R packages, facilitating seamless integration of new tools and algorithms within the COPASI interface. Users can explore our framework and download ShinyCOPASI for free at copasi.org.

This research introduces a novel method to quantify uncertainty in machine learning as applied to scientific data analysis, with the aim of contributing to the advancement of open science by bridging the gaps between data, methods, and results. A systematic review revealed a lack of consensus on ambiguity metrics, leading to the development of the Ambiguity Analysis Framework (AAF) which comprises three key components: data, computational methods, and artistic interpretation. Within this framework, three distinct measurement approaches to ambiguity are described in detail, each corresponding to a different layer of the framework. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed methods revealed that their performance in identifying unambiguous models surpasses that of existing uncertainty quantification techniques, solidifying the claim that these novel methods effectively measure ambiguity within the context of the Ambiguity Analysis Framework.

We are investigating the closure of the set of category functions on a compact quantum group, denoted as ${\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)$. The paper provides functional inequalities that define a von Neumann algebra containing ${\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)$. The study also involves identifying a subalgebra within this larger algebra and computing its relative atomicity. Specifically, we demonstrate that the closure of ${\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)$ is a subset of $M_{2p^\!*}({\mathcal B}^{\mathrm{op}}\overline{\Delta})'$. Moreover, we define a subalgebra $({\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H)\otimes {\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H))_s$ as the closure of $(x\otimes y)s$ for all $x,y\in {\mathcal C}^\mathrm{cat}(H), s\in S$. We prove that this subalgebra has relative atomicity equal to $\frac{1}{2p^\!*} M_{2p^\!*}({\mathcal B}^{\mathrm{op}}\overline{\Delta})'$.

Solving massive-scale Markov decision processes (MDPs) poses significant computational challenges, primarily due to the need for repeated inverse operations in value iteration. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in extensive form MDPs, where the inverse matrix must be computed multiple times per step. To address this issue, we have adapted the GMRES method to provide an alternative solution for solving linear equations in value iteration. However, the high variability in communication requirements led us to develop an alternative strategy, namely the impulsive GMRES strategy, which offers superior performance to the current best approaches and is highly adaptable, with a theoretical guarantee of convergence to the optimal policy. Moreover, our method exhibits cost efficiency and sequential communication optimality. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the robustness and performance benefits of this method, particularly in scenarios with large state spaces and few actions per state.

This research examines the properties of algebraic and combinatorial nature in the edge ideals of directed graphs, particularly focusing on line graphs and linear spaces, as well as pseudolinear spaces and point-line configurations. Our study reveals both similarities and differences between these edge ideals and line ideal properties. As an extension, we investigate the symbolic powers of these edge ideals, determining when isomorphism is maintained under various circumstances.

When modeling complex systems through computer simulations, researchers often encounter a challenging inverse problem: inferring a physical parameter from a simulation output, especially when the simulation itself is subject to uncertainty. For example, heat transfer experiments using infrared thermometry can be hampered by low resolution thermometry data, which hinders researchers from accurately determining the temperature distribution in the object of interest. To overcome this problem, we employ a multi-step approach, combining the approximation of a high-dimensional parameter by minimizing a difference in data and a statistical comparison of the results using a Bayesian framework. Specifically, we approximate a high-dimensional parameter through an optimization process that treats noise in the data as random, then conduct a Bayesian comparison of the results to account for the inherent randomness. Ultimately, our method allows researchers to conduct a statistical comparison of the simulated heat transfer and actual measurements to inform the parameter estimation process.

To minimize the impact of malicious models, resilient learning has a collective goal of achieving accurate classification while preventing private information extraction. A promising approach to achieve this is called Region-Based Resilient Learning, which incorporates geographical regions in the learning process and has previously demonstrated advantageous results. However, the underlying assumption of this method relies on the presence of beneficial regional queries, without justifying their existence or functionality in the context of resilient learning. This study justifies the existence and utility of regional queries, revealing that they contain valuable information for improving model accuracy and reducing dependence on external data sources. Furthermore, this information can also be harnessed by an adversary to compromise learning accuracy, highlighting a previously unexplored dynamic within resilient learning. Based on these findings, a strategic decision-making model is proposed, encouraging learners to trust regional queries only when the potential benefits outweigh the risks posed by potential leakage.

High-energy particles known as jets that form in certain areas of a collision event can be influenced by the surrounding material. In central collisions, where the density of the material is densest, it's been observed that jet production is altered, but research suggests it's primarily a result of the material's density and not a genuine alteration to the jets themselves. However, studies have also indicated that the fragments making up these jets may be affected as well. In a new study, researchers utilized data from the CMS experiment at the LHC to investigate changes to the structure of these jets. They focused on areas of the collisions where photons, high-energy particles that don't interact, are present, which helps to rule out any alterations to the jets themselves. They found that in addition to being affected, the fragments of these jets also experience changes in their movement. What's more, these changes continue even after the material's influence has ceased to be felt.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of evaluating sums of hypergeometric functions, particularly those with alternating signs. Such series are a modified version of the Apéry-type series initially studied by Apéry and later by a multitude of mathematicians and physicists. A recent series of papers by the author delves into a specific category of these sums that involve colored multiple zeta functions. This current installation continues to explore one particular subclass of 5-variable sums that involve alternating signs in both the numerator and denominator of the color factors. It confirms that this subclass can be expressed through the application of the fundamental theorem of colored multiple zeta functions by demonstrating the equivalence between their respective expansion forms.

We introduced WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, a peculiar object initially identified as a low-frequency variable source with a brown dwarf spectrum, and presented our photometric data and spectroscopic observations from multiple telescopes. The object's peculiar behavior remains unexplained despite our findings and theoretical analyses, and our study remains inconclusive due to the presence of a power flux distribution not seen in brown dwarfs, and mismatched spectral patterns between observed and predicted spectra.

The mean multiplicities of specific mesons and baryons emitted in relativistic Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV are calculated using the ALPINO detector's acceptance properties. This is accomplished by incorporating the ALPINO's identification efficiency and track count limitations into a relativistic transport model. Resulting mean multiplicities of produced particles show minimal variation with respect to changing Xe-Xe collision geometries, thus yielding readily interpretable results. Mean multiplicities of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons are determined and compared to current experimental measurements, revealing notable agreement between results.

We've developed a novel method to progress and interpolate parton distribution functions at varying scales by utilizing machine learning in an unsupervised manner. This technique doesn't require explicit knowledge of the parton distribution functions' evolution equations or their precise values at adjacent scales. Moreover, it can be applied across the entire range of x, without needing prior knowledge of relevant functions' properties. This method efficiently retrieves critical information from parton distribution functions' evolution constraints, ultimately resulting in accurate PDF predictions at different scales. Notably, this technique is versatile and can be applied to various distribution functions, such as universal and non-universal PDFs, as well as to different flavor channels. Our approach is also computationally efficient, allowing direct PDF evaluations at any x and scale with minimal computational cost.

For establishing and sustaining life on other planets, it's crucial to utilize in situ manufacturing techniques that can create versatile materials from local resources. A method called powder bed fusion enables the production of complex shapes from planetary regolith powders, thereby allowing the formation of essential infrastructure like habitats and solar panels. This study examines how heat treatment affects the mechanical and microstructural properties of fused samples made from regolith powders collected from Hawaii, representing lunar samples, and Paterson Mesa, standing in for Martian samples. X-ray computed tomography revealed the internal faults of the regolith powders, which significantly affect their mechanical properties, with strengths in the range of 0.5 to 40 MPa, far below those of conventional construction materials. Moreover, heat treatment between 800-1100°C improved the mechanical properties, with gains up to 300% for Hawaii samples and 500% for Paterson Mesa samples, thus significantly impacting the 3D printing process parameters and the subsequent heat treatment procedure. A thorough understanding of these influences is necessary for creating infrastructure on other planets using 3D printing techniques.

We're investigating the dynamics of a liquid droplet forming on a fiber as part of the Rayleigh-Plateau instability process. Our approach combines linear analysis and numerical simulations with a focus on the role of surface slip. The results suggest that surface slip has a significant impact on the droplet formation process, leading to differences in droplet size and shape. Additionally, we've identified new instability mechanisms influenced by slip, along with the consequences of surface tension variations. Our research provides a framework for understanding droplet formation processes through the lens of slip effects.

By comparing observed data and model predictions for galaxies at a specific distance, we can assess the reliability of different methods for estimating star formation rates. Past research has established that rear-facing ionizing radiation, specifically at 1458 Angstrom, Brackett-$\gamma$, can be an effective indicator of these rates, as it is less affected by dust. Nevertheless, using this emission line for this purpose in distant galaxies is complicated because the signal is often weakened due to absorption within our own galaxy. In a study published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics, we present our findings on how SED fitting can relate to Brackett-$\gamma$ emission in a collection of around 3700 galaxies, all located between 0.02 and 0.5 redshift. By applying the PRODIGAL SED-fitting code to a collection of around 1000 artificial galaxies, we validated that the model's estimated star formation rates are closely aligned with the observed emission lines, including Brackett-$\gamma$. In a wide range of galaxy types, our analysis found a strong correlation between the predicted and observed Brackett-$\gamma$ emission, with a scatter consistent with other established indicators. Moreover, we found that using strong rear-facing ionization can improve the SED fit and resulting star formation rate estimates, especially in galaxies that are both distant and heavily obscured. In a wide range of galaxy types, our analysis found a strong correlation between the predicted and observed Brackett-$\gamma$ emission,

In the realm of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$, a subtle pattern has been observed, where a high level type $II$ quantum subalgebra is generated from the tensor product of two copies of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, aligning with Kirillov-Suris' universal type $II$ construction. To uncover this non-degenerate structure, we delve into the representation of regional modules within type $II$ quantum subalgebras, revealing the essential components of base modules and $\mathbb{Z}_2$-invariant sectors. This work also establishes connections between the type $II$ subalgebra's central elements and Suris' symmetries of regional modules, offering a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between these symmetries and the type $II$ subalgebra itself. Furthermore, at high levels, the region-based structure of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$'s type $II$ quantum subalgebras is related to the Weyl group $W_{N+1}$.

The unified approach to diffusion reveals the fundamental equation governing the diffusion process, which is based on the average rate of change in energy. This rate is influenced by the rate of molecular motion, the magnitude of the thermal coefficient, and the time variable, and is derived through a straightforward mathematical procedure. This coefficient may be thought of as a temperature-dependent equivalent to the standard diffusion coefficient, and its measurement value for carbon dioxide is approximately 0.3 centimeters squared per second. This result agrees with empirical data, and the proposed theoretical framework offers a novel and fundamental understanding of the diffusion process.

Recent advancements in mobile technology have enabled the collection of detailed data on tactile handwriting via high-resolution sensors embedded in styluses, tablets, and touchscreens. By capturing additional information beyond what standard pen technology could record, these advanced sensors have the potential to revolutionize the field of handwriting analysis. Specifically, we've discovered that by leveraging the data from these sensors, we can efficiently distinguish between different handwritten mathematical expressions, like fractions, roots, and squares, as well as identify various mathematical operators like plus, minus, and multiplication. By utilizing a combination of sensor-driven data and machine learning techniques, we've been able to achieve remarkable accuracy in classification, reaching levels as high as 85% on the expressions and 90% on the operators, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods that relied solely on video capture and hand-crafted features, which resulted in lower accuracy rates of 55% and 70%, respectively. Therefore, it appears that sensor-driven data has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of handwriting analysis.

This study proposes a novel approach to generate synthetic speech lengths by leveraging a non-parametric statistical method called the Median Absolute Deviation algorithm. Initially, a group of speakers' speech lengths are collected and the median value is calculated to represent the target length for the model. The median absolute deviation is then used to determine the acceptable range for speech segment durations. The proposed method is evaluated in two domains: conversation and monologue, and demonstrates efficacy in modeling various speech length distributions observed in human speakers.

Species distribution models are used in various biological research applications, such as habitat selection studies which can be single species, involving multiple species, or combining individual species models with habitat models. We introduce spHabitat, an R package that efficiently computes single species, multi species, and integrated habitat models using binary and continuous presence-only data. We then demonstrate the efficacy of this package through comparative studies of presence-only models, focusing on binary data. Furthermore, we highlight its capabilities for running single species, multi species, and combined models, utilizing simulated data. spHabitat is an open-source package that is a part of the spHabitat R package on CRAN.

The Skincare initiative is a collaborative project between academic and industrial partners, focused on integrating artificial intelligence into dermatology practice. This report outlines the project's core objectives, which center on the incorporation of deep learning methods to support the differential diagnosis of skin cancers. Specifically, the team is utilizing a dataset of images, gathered from the Dermatology Image Analysis dataset on the First Place challenge hosted by the IEEE International Conference on Image Analysis and Processing. These images comprise a vital dataset for training deep neural networks to distinguish between malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and other benign skin lesions.

One of the primary objectives in cosmology is to determine the density of dark energy by tracking the expansion of the universe. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers have been studying type Ia supernovae because of their consistent explosion patterns, which allow for precise calibration. Nevertheless, the inherent unpredictability in supernovae explosions complicates this process. To tackle this challenge, scientists proposed utilizing recurrent neural networks, but a significant issue arose: the trade-off between precise spectra readings and overall sequence prediction accuracy. To address this limitation, researchers suggested utilizing pre-trained autoencoders, but once again, the issue of inherent randomness in supernovae spectra data persisted. To overcome this hurdle, the authors of this research paper presented an innovative stochastic autoencoder, which seamlessly combined to avoid compromising either spectra quality or sequence prediction quality. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the authors conducted a series of experiments using a publicly available dataset of 1041 type Ia supernovae spectra sequences. To simulate randomness in the data, the authors employed a simple Gaussian process. The results showed that the proposed stochastic autoencoder outperformed its classical counterpart in sequence prediction, while also producing high-quality reconstructed spectra with improved Charlier parameters.

A massive, neutral gas cloud is being ejected from a distant, star-forming galaxy. The galaxy, located at a distance of approximately 2.09 billion light-years, is part of an ongoing research project examining the formation of galaxies at early stages of their evolution. The observed galaxy is one of the most intensely active star-forming galaxies discovered so far, with its light is amplified by a massive gravitational lens. The measurement suggests that a large amount of neutral gas is being expelled from the galaxy at high speeds, exceeding 500 kilometers per second in some cases. This phenomenon is most pronounced in the galaxy's central areas, with its impact most intense at wavelengths of around 500-600 nanometers. The observed gas cloud is growing larger, with its diameter increasing by approximately 400 parsecs every year. The most intense neutral gas emission is becoming weaker, while the proportion of dust in the emission is remaining relatively stable. The galaxy's overall mass is estimated to be in the range of 10^11 to 10^12 times the mass of our sun, with its rate of mass loss in the range of 10-100 times the mass of our sun per year. The rate of mass loss is not affected by the galaxy's overall mass, with its value approximately equal to a constant.
